title: What Actually Makes me think
excerpt: Reflections on asymmetric returns, winner-take-all markets, and the power of time in investing.
content:
As I was reading black swan again the similar realization of Asymmetric return came to mind. About how a lot of thing in life is zero sum and just a fraction better and luck makes all the difference in distribution of wealth, Fame, Power. Person making billion dollar should not necessarily be 1000x more smart or hard working or capable than person making 1 million.

There might be million singers but just fractionally better singers gets all the attention and listening cause why listen 10% less objectively melodious music when you can listen to the very best.

The thing about working in unpredictable sector is you might crawl 30 years and in one fine year you will make all the return that you didn't in precious 30 years. This is not typically true for people working in job or something that doesn't have black swan events.

World operates in winner take all method in so many way. Also working in a field like investing is a highly leverage field. You can make 1 million or 1 thousand with same insights idea or research.

I think investing is belief changing career. And it's hard to have a hypothesis or belief about something today and immediately change it tomorrow it takes time. So time is a real edge in this field. Also the reason changing a hypothesis too quick is difficult is you need to test it and it requires feedback loop which again requires time and attention over a period of time. You can't force yourself to be highly iterative and functional. You will slowly realize how stupid and dumb you were to invest or trade two years back and you come to this realization with slow feedback.

id: the need for a mental gym
title: The Need For A Mental GYM
excerpt: How the struggle for critical thinking will be a serious issue.
content:
If we were to fundamentally distinguish our life and daily existence, we would simply divide it into two parts: the physical body and the cognitive or mental body. From our earliest history to today, significant transformations have occurred, particularly in our relationship with nutrition and information transformations that have created profound imbalances in both spheres. 

 Historically, humans transitioned from struggling to find enough food for survival to now facing the challenge of overconsumption and excess calories. This shift reveals fascinating evolutionary adaptations and misalignments. From an evolutionary perspective, our craving for carbohydrates and sugar made sense during hunting-gathering times when such resources were rare. Our bodies were constantly in motion, searching for food and energy, with physical mobility being a natural, necessary daily activity. Today, we have unrestricted access to carbs and sugar, but without the corresponding physical effort required to obtain them. 

 To compensate for this imbalance, we've created artificial environments like gyms to simulate the physical exertion our ancestors experienced naturally. We've shifted from being energy-conservative to energy extensive, from preserving calories to intentionally burning them. This conscious adaptation demonstrates our ability to recognize and address physical imbalances when they become apparent. 

 Interestingly, a similar transformation has occurred in our cognitive landscape, but with a crucial difference. While we've developed structured solutions for physical fitness, our approach to information consumption remains largely unstructured. 

We're inundated with information much of which triggers our primitive instincts like sex and violence that once served crucial survival functions but now exists in overwhelming abundance without context. Just as we overeat without physical exertion, we overconsume information without mental processing. 

 Unlike physical health, where we've created gyms and fitness programs, we haven't developed equivalent systems for cognitive fitness no mental gym to help us process, filter, and truly understand information. This gap has led to significant information asymmetry in society, where access to quality information and the ability to process it meaningfully aren't equally distributed. We've become mental consumers rather than knowledge processors. 

 As our world grows increasingly complex, many remain trapped in simplified narratives. While some segments of society develop advanced technologies like AI, others lack the foundational knowledge to question basic assumptions. This growing divide isn't just about access to information it's about the ability to understand and utilize it effectively. Like physical malnourishment in a world of food abundance, we face cognitive malnourishment in a world of information abundance. 

 The stories we consume and the content we engage with shape both individual understanding and collective societal thinking. Just as we've become conscious of our physical diet, we need to be mindful of our information diet. In a world where information flows endlessly, the quality of what we consume matters more than ever. Yet, unlike calories we haven't learned to measure, balance or optimize our information intake. 

 The path forward lies in recognizing that information, like nutrition, requires both quantity and quality. Through collective curiosity and shared learning, we can begin to understand the basic mechanisms of how our world works. Small communities of curious minds, sharing insights and fostering meaningful discussions, might be the first step toward developing better ways to process and understand the world around us. Just as we learned to balance our physical consumption, we must now learn to balance our mental consumption creating not just informed individuals, but wisely informed societies.

title: Investing In Early Business
excerpt: Reflections on why investing in early business or project will always beat investing in easily assessable businesses.
content:
One thing I have underestimated is how hard it is to consistently make good returns over the long term even being very active in the market. The only way to make amazing returns in the long term is to get invested in a company that is just getting started. There is a different kind of opportunity and risk involved in getting in early, but fundamentally, that is the only way to achieve returns in multiples. 

 I saw a message today from a person who invested 1.3 crore for short term trading and made around 8 to 9% profit. After taxation, commission, and everything else, it would probably turn out to be around 10 lakh. 

 But for a person to consistently make a 10% return in the short term is fundamentally impossible. So even compounding 1.3 crore into 4 to 5 crore over the next 4 to 5 years is a job that seems quite difficult and hectic. But I feel the opportunity lies in companies that are just getting started. Think about someone who invested 1 crore in a hydro project without any prior knowledge of investing and just let the capital remain invested in the project. That investment could easily turn into 3 to 4 crore in the next 5 years. This is something we are missing completely, and the major reason is psychological. 

 Investing in the early days and just leaving the capital invested does not give us the feeling that the capital is working because we are not exposed to it on a daily basis. We are also not actively contributing or using our headspace to help the money compound, so it feels like something that will not work for us. 

 But after all these years of reflection, I have come to the conclusion that I should give all my energy towards finding opportunities that are not easily available to everyone and take the risk with the belief that it will somehow work. But that belief should not come from the idea of luck. It should come from enough preparation to find the right insights and the ability to predict whether it will work or not.

 Almost every individual or institution that has made massive wealth has generated more than 90% of that wealth by investing in early companies or projects where the valuation was minimal.

 Just think and reflect back. Even in my own experience, if I look at the return compared to the capital deployed, it is very hard to make good returns by investing at competitive valuations where the upside potential is very limited.

 But still, why is it hard for us to invest in something and wait for years, if not a decade? 

 Again, it is psychological because it does not offer predictability, instant liquidity, or certainty. More importantly, it does not give us the feeling of being productive. We are used to being active, and investing and trading every day gives us that feeling of active and engaged hence productive. 

 Think about having 1 crore in capital and somehow finding the right opportunity to invest in an early stage project that other people are building. What if I invest the whole 1 crore and suddenly it becomes illiquid, and I have nothing to trade or invest in? 

 This exact feeling is why we keep investing or trading on a daily basis. 

 It is the same thing if you are doing investing as a full time job. But if you start working a new full time job, that new job might give you the feeling of being engaged and productive, so you might neglect the other part, which is investing. I could see that happening around me. 

 So now the idea is to put enormous energy and time into finding rare opportunities in early stage projects and find enough courage to leave the capital invested for the next 5 to 10 years

title: Are We Facing Economic Slowdown Or Just Being More Cautious?
excerpt: Reflections on economic cycle and how short-term downtrend creates a lot of fear mongering among investors.
content:
When we invest in equities we are basically investing in a business. The stock price is only a representation of what that business does, its sales, its costs, and its ability to convert all that effort into profit. If we look one layer deeper we can see a connection between three things, how a business performs, how the broader economy is doing, and how equity prices move. These three things don't always move together. 

 Right now, the Nepali market is in a downtrend. Most of the sectors look like they are consolidating. And when we are inside a downtrend, our brain naturally gives more importance to recent events and recent experiences. So we start feeling more pessimistic than the actual situation might justify. This is just a normal human tendency. 

 My underlying belief is that human society as a whole always moves towards progress. People want to make more money, build better lives, provide better lives for their families, and improve the things around them. As long as this basic human drive exists, consumption will keep increasing over time. It will not happen in a straight line, but the long term direction will still be towards growth. 

 If I do not believe this, then the whole exercise of investing would be pointless. Because at the end of the day investing is basically a bet on future consumption and future profits.

 If we accept that the economy eventually grows, consumption eventually increases, and good companies eventually make more money, then the basic logic of investing remains the same. But like everything else, the economy moves in cycles and investing also follows these cycles.

 There are certain periods when people prefer to keep their money safe (In banks or relatively safe assets) rather than put it into productive activities. This is real and we can see it happening. But it cannot continue forever. If it did, everyone would simply keep their money in gold or other safe assets and no one would ever come back to equities. 

 I think we are naturally wired to seek growth and productivity, not permanent safety. Right now, what we are seeing is that money is more focused on protection rather than productive use. But money does not stay there forever. It eventually starts flowing towards wherever it can be used productively. It can go into businesses, markets, new projects, or new ventures./n/n If this flow completely stopped and money stayed stuck in safety forever, then I would say we have a much bigger problem. That would mean something structurally wrong is happening in the country, possibly a real economic slowdown or even a deflationary consumption cycle. 

 But I don't see evidence of that happening in Nepal right now. 

 So my view remains that good days are ahead. But being hopeful does not mean blindly believing that everything will be fine. We actually need to look at what is happening around us. 

 Has real economic activity slowed down? 

 Has actual consumption decreased? 

 Are businesses fundamentally earning less because people have stopped spending? 

 If the honest answer to these questions is no, then I still believe investing in good businesses should deliver returns over time. 

 Because the underlying engine is still running. People are still working, earning, spending, and businesses are still converting that activity into profits. The economy has not stopped working. It is simply going through a phase where money is more cautious. 

 And I think there is a big difference between a period where money is cautious and a period where the economy itself has actually broken down. If consumption really sholws down there will be signs and I have a hint of doubt sometime because the age group with most consumption ability are moving abroad but again it's too early.. So be hopeful invest in business which actually makes money.
